explainBack.question: Why doesn't a school's existing Microsoft subscription automatically protect student data in every Microsoft tool teachers and students use?
explainBack.answer: Two gates must both open. First, the agreement only covers education-designed generative AI products; general productivity, communications, search and workplace-assistance tools are excluded by definition even when the school licenses them. Second, the protections are not automatic: the district must opt in by requesting that the standard's terms be incorporated into its own Microsoft agreement, which is what makes them contractually enforceable. A teacher's general work assistant fails the first gate; a district that never requested incorporation fails the second.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The article's scope definition and exclusion (P003), the incorporation-makes-enforceable mechanism (P002), and the tutor-versus-work-assistant illustration (P007).
explainBack.assessment: Accurate and complete from article content alone; the two-gate causal structure is stated explicitly in P002-P003 and dramatized in P007, so the mechanism supports explain-back without external sources.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A district's library offers students a Microsoft general-purpose AI search assistant for research, while its English department deploys a Microsoft AI writing tutor built and marketed for classrooms. The district signed the standard into its Microsoft agreement last month. A librarian asks whether student queries in both tools are protected from training use.
unseenTransfer.question: Which tool's student data is covered by the no-training and companion-feature protections, and why?
unseenTransfer.answer: Only the writing tutor. The district cleared the opt-in gate by incorporating the standard, but the standard attaches per product: the tutor is an education-designed generative AI product, so student prompts and outputs in it cannot be used for model training (beyond the narrow safety exception) and companion-style features are banned. The general search assistant is excluded by the scope definition even though the same district licenses it from the same vendor, so its protections come only from whatever ordinary terms govern that product.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: P003's exclusion of general search and workplace-assistance products, P002's incorporation mechanism, and P004's training prohibition applying to covered information.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism resolves this new scenario decisively: product scope and opt-in operate independently, and applying both gates yields a specific, correct answer — genuine transfer succeeded.

announcement.reason: Microsoft release is dated Sept. 9, 2026 and jointly announces the standard with AFT President Weingarten and UFT President Mulgrew, matching the article.

enforceable-request.reason: Microsoft announcement states verbatim that U.S. school districts can incorporate these protections directly into their Microsoft customer agreements, making them contractually enforceable.

opt-in.reason: MOA applies principles to 'an EDU Customer who has opted in' and requires districts to request incorporation via the provider's request process ('a district can make the request at any time'), supporting the opt-in framing.

scope.reason: MOA's definition of AI Provider Educational Products expressly excludes general-purpose productivity, collaboration, communication, search, cloud, development, or workplace-assistance products even when licensed by educational entities.

training-limits.reason: MOA Purpose-Limited Use clause bars data under the safety exception from general model training or improvement, advertising, market research, unrelated products, or other commercial purposes — matching the article.

companion.reason: MOA prohibits companion-style or relationship-oriented features designed to foster emotional attachment or dependency or to keep students engaged longer than the learning task requires (L318-321).

telemetry.reason: MOA Telemetry Data definition permits use for security, reliability, service health and product improvements but prohibits generative-model training, student profiling, and behavioral inference — matching the article's summary.

criticism.reason: AP reports Golin of Fairplay called protections meaningful but said the agreement sidesteps whether AI products belong in classrooms or at what age; attribution to AP is retained in the article.

other-vendors.reason: AP reports OpenAI and Anthropic said they were discussing safety and privacy pacts with AFT, while Google has not said whether it plans to offer similar protections — matching the article with AP attribution.

accuracy.reason: MOA requires the product to 'provide clear, age-appropriate notices that AI outputs may be incorrect' (L339-340), directly supporting the article's claim.
